author: ohtadmin
title: Show using seeds, shells, stones on display
text:
A display of mandalas created with natural materials by a Tiverton artist is being featured at the Jamestown Philomenian Library through Feb. 20.
Meredith Brower, who is an ecological artist and photographer, creates her mandalas using shells, stones, sea glass, feathers, twigs, grass, leaves and seed pods she finds near her farm. She then photographs the pattern she has created and puts most of the material back into the environment.
The gallery at the library features around 20 of Brower’s mandala photographs. She was chosen to display by Jillian Barber, a Jamestown ceramicist who has curated exhibitions at the library for nearly 30 years.
Brower is a professional photographer whose work has appeared in The Newport Daily News and Newport Life magazine. She started making the mandalas about 10 years ago after a friend suggested she investigate the work of British sculptor Andy Goldsworthy. That sparked Brower’s interest in an artistic movement that addresses ecological concerns, or “eco-art,” and challenged herself to make a mandala every day for a year.
During the next year, Brower spent part of each day foraging and collecting material, arranging them into mandalas, and photographing the results.
“It wasn’t necessarily the work I got out of it,” she said. “It was the time I allotted to myself to be creative.”
At first, the work was something Brower did just for herself. After a year, her sister suggested she make cards featuring the photographs. Those cards got a good reception, and her friends that owned stores asked if they could sell them. She also kept making mandalas and started printing them on aluminum pans or as Giclee digital prints.
Brower makes her mandalas with a wide variety of items she finds on her farm that she jokingly refers to as “lovely dead crap.” The items she on both a seasonal basis.
“When I do go out and I photograph, sometimes I have an intention of what I want to focus on,” she said. “A color or a size. Other times, I have no intention and I’m just waiting for the inspiration to land underneath my feet.”
When making the mandalas, Brower starts with the background and builds up into the foreground.
Brower said she wants everything to look neat and organized, and in specific patterns. Sometimes the design is loose; other times, tight. There also are variables like the wind, which may scatter the items she is working with, or her cats, which are simply curious about what she is doing outside.
Brower said the foraging is the best part of making the mandalas because it brings her outside, which gives her a different perspective while looking for material.
“If you can stop your brain from judging your heart, and make decisions that way, it’s sort of this warm, fuzzy area that you can function in and be creative,” Brower said.
Once she is finished photographing the mandalas, Brower disassembles and throws most of the material back into the fields. She describes the mandalas as “ephemeral or impermanent art.”
However, there are a few special objects she has kept and used in multiple mandalas. These include a pair of antlers that have recurred in a series of photographs, four of which are on display at the library.
A pair of gallery openings resulted in Brower’s library display. Brower and Barber met after they displayed their work at back-to-back show at the Hunter Gallery at St. George’s School in Middletown. Brower’s nephew, Jonathan, is an art teacher at the private school and curates that space. He had an opening right after Barber’s show, Brower took that spot.
“It just worked out perfectly,” Brower said.
The pieces in the show were selected by Barber due to their size, color and weight. Barber said the repeating patterns and concentric circles of mandalas exist in many cultures, including Buddhist, Hindu and Native American traditions.
“Gazing upon the image helps to focus the mind,” she said. “Meredith’s eye grazes along the lushness of the earth choosing textures of leaves, petals of flowers, feathers, rocks, shells and bones to create her mandalas, and with an artist’s eye, she assembles earth’s delicate treasures and natural bounty.”
Barber said she and Brower share a common interest in collecting antlers, shells and heart-shaped rocks.
“We are earth girls,” Barber said.
The gallery is the first time Brower has been displayed in Jamestown.
“The space is wonderful,” she said. “It’s got great light, plenty of space, and it was really easy to put up.”
Brower’s work can be found at shops in Rhode Island and Massachusetts, including Hotpoint Emporium in Bristol and Whimsies in Warren. She also has a website, Firefly Mandalas, and an Instagram account with that same name.
